To provide for a fisheries exhibit at the Canadian National Exhibition at Toronto, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I explained this item fully last night. If my hon. friends require any further information, I shall be very glad to give it to them. Our expenditure in 1914-15 was $12,417.89, and the expenditure up to the 31st of December, 1915, was $10,732.87. We were given $15,000 last year;, this year we are asking for $10,000. I sent to my hon. friends opposite a copy of the bill of fare, which was changed every day. The total cost to us of running the restaurant was $3,251.

It is refreshing to find an item of this kind in looking over the fishery Estimates, because we usually find pretty much the same old thing stated in the same old way year after year. This is an item, however, that is calculated to do a great deal of good, and it has already done a great deal of good. Last year I visited the Toronto Exhibition, and it was a matter of great pride and pleasure to me to hear the words of commendation spoken on all sides regarding the fisheries exhibit.
It is gratifying indeed to find that the minister is doing something in this regard. But one swallow does not make a summer; and, while we may commend the minister for this particular appropriation. I am afraid that if we analyse what has been done in the department it' will be found that all the encomiums that have been
heaped upon him by some of the sycophants of his department and published in a Montreal magazine a short time ago are not justified,-they are largely of the sounding brass and tinkling cymbals variety. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) last night drew the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the way in which the fisheries are given a black eye in the dining car service of the Intercolonial. I would direct the attention of the minister further to the evidence given a short time ago before the special committee of this House on the Fisheries. I do not wish to go into that evidence now, because this is not the time for it. But when you find a man like Mr. Alfred H. Brittain, who, I understand, is chairman of the transportation committee of the Canadian Fisheries Association, and also a member of the transportation committee of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, saying that the manner in which the Intercolonial is helping out the fisheries of the country is simply deplorable, and, in fact, worse than that, you realize that the situation is not all that it ought to be. Mr. Brittain declares that he never could undersand why they dropped the refrigerator and cold storage service on the Intercolonial. This service was established by the late Government but it was dropped by the present Administration. And we are told by Mr. D. J. Byrne, President of the Canadian Fisheries Association, that the refrigerator service was dropped. So, instead of going ahead, we are going back. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) pointed out that there had been no advance, no real progress, made in the fishing industry in a quarter of a century. The attempt was made a few years ago to make progress by the inauguration of a refrigerator express service, but the present Minister of Railways out that out. Of course, he blamed it on the war-everything is blamed on the war. But nobody takes any stock in that. The fact is, the Minister of Railways is not in sympathy with the idea, he is not in sympathy with the people of the Maritime Provinces. That is apparent in the whole operation of the Intercolonial, from the appointment of officials at the head of it down throughout the whole service.
What I rose for was to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the necessity of waking up the Minister of Railways and getting him to put us back where we were before. If he cannot get the Minister of Railways to help in

the efforts (o advance the fishing industry, let him try to check that hon. gentleman in doing injury and in thwarting the efforts of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries h'mself. The Minister of Railways, by the manner in which he has treated the refrigerator-oar service, and in the way he conducts the dining-car service on the Intercolonial, has done a great deal of injury to the cause.

Surely my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. William Chisholm) is sufficiently serious to demand an answer from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Gan it be true that the Minister of Railways has abandoned the express service fo- fish from the Maritime Provinces? Surely that cannot be true.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, that is not the case.
Then, I think the minister should explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The whole matter appears in the report of the department of this year. There are two branches to the complaint of my hon. friend from Antigonish. One is the price charged for fish in the dining cars of the Intercolonial.
And the quality.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The point made by the hon. mentber for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) last night was the price. But I think the same price prevails now as has prevailed since the a la carte service was introduced, and the same as on the Canadian Pacific railway and other lines in competition with the Intercolonial.. But in any case, that is a matter to which the attention of the Department of Railways should foe drawn. As to express service charges, the report says:
It was the hope of the department that when it was shown to the express companies that a large business could be done in the transportation of fresh and mildly cured fish, if proper facilities and cheap enough rates were made available, they would afford such, and the Government would thus he relieved of the necessity for paying any portion of the charges.
This policy was adopted years before I came into office.
Up to the moment, they have shown no-disposition to reduce their rates;-
That matter has been thoroughly thrashed out by the Committee on Marine and Fisheries that will report in a day or two:

-hut even if they do not, experience is indicating that the time is approaching when the business will foe large enough to enafole it to he handled practically altogether in refrigerator cars hauled by fast freight. Shipments now going forward in such cars reach their destination in perfect condition, which is not always the case with consignments packed in ice in ordinary express cars. Already the shipments brought from Canso-via Mulgrave-and Halifax for the Friday markets in Montreal, Toronto, etc., have reached carload proportions, and are regularly forwarded in refrigerator cars by fast freight. Indeed, the only difficulty to having the daily shipments forwarded by fast freight is the late date at which the wholesale dealers are able to procure their orders. What seems to he needed then is the education hy the wholesalers of the retailers to the desirability, in their own interests, of the latter placing their orders a few days in advance-By so doing they will not only he assured of receiving their fish in perfect condition, but at cheaper prices than if forwarded by the more expensive express method.
In other words, the advice is given to dealers, now that the business is reaching such large proportions, and the freight service is so satisfactory with the refrigerator cars, that they should have their fish forwarded in that way rather than by express cars, in which the service is not as good as it should he-I have no hesitation in saying that, for there has been considerable criticism of the service-and in which it costs thepi more than by the freight cars. The express service is still available, $s it has been.

Evidently the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is ready to take the statement of the theorists of his department as against the evidence of practical, common sense men, who know what they are talking about. Let him refer to the evidence of Mr. Brittain, to whom I have referred. I do not want to go into the evidence, but evidently the minister is entirely under a misapprehension as to the facts, so far as the Intercolonial is concerned, and needs enlightenment on the subject. Therefore I venture to refer to a matter that has not yet been reported upon, although in doing so I may be out of order. I wish to refer to No. 1 of the official report, taken on Monday, February 21, 1916. Mr. McCurdy asks Mr. Brittain the following question:
What is the reason the refrigerator express service was dropped? Was there not sufficient volume of business?
The answer is:
I could never understand up to this day why' that service was dropped. I believe it was the nucleus to a successful operation; it was the

forerunner of the freight service; it gradually introduced the fast freight service.
There is evidence that the service was dropped. Again, toy referring to page 7, we see how much encouragement is being given to the fishing industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want to go into this matter, because it has not been reported upon, tout if the hon. gentleman wishes to go into it he ought to read the statement made by Mr. Found on that very point.

With all due respect to Mr. Found, I prefer to take the evidence of Mr. Brittain, who is familiar with the practical side of this question.' No doubt Mr. Found is an expert on fish, but when it copies to the question of transportation I do not know who is in a better position to give evidence than Mr. Brittain. He says further:
The whole trouble, in so far as I can see it, is that there is no encouragement given to "fresh, perishable and mildly cured fish through a fast freight service.
I am finding fault, not with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, tout with the Minister of Railways. On page 8 Mr. Brittain gives the following evidence:
Q. Now you are speaking of express cars?- A. Yes.
Q. Now what about freights?-A. In so far as freight is concerned, I am now referring to the Maritime Provinces; up till within four months ago we had a very satisfactory service on the Canadian Government railways, but unfortunately since then they have been overloaded with business through a condition arising from the war which we have in Europe.
He states that in so far as freight is concerned they had a satisfactory service up to four months ago; unfortunately, the service got bad, at that time. Again, at page 38, Mr. Byrne, President of the Canadian Fisheries Association, gives evidence to the effect that we are not getting a satisfactory service:
Q. The main point, you say, is this: that you pay the express companies high rates for a good service and that they are not in return giving you the service that you are entitled to. Is there any other way out of it? Instead of running your fish through the private express companies, is there a way out by the Intercolonial keeping the business in its own hands? Do you think it would be possible for it to do so?-A. I think the best method of handling the fish business Is by developing it and by increasing the shipments offer; the best means of improving the transportation would be for the railway companies to give a better service, a refrigerator freight service; they should provide refrigerator cars, properly built, properly iced and give a quick service.	,
2417
Q. A quick freight service?-A. A quick freight service, and make it a really quick service. They could improve it a great deal; there is no reason why there should be so much difference in time between express and freight. We have had it proven in connection with other commodities, where we have competition, that they can give a quicker service.
Later on toe speaks of the kind of service they get down there. It is a fact that it takes six or seven days for fish to get from the Maritime Provinces to Montreal. That is not exceptional; it occurs quite frequently. The complaint of the dealers in fish in the large cities is that the transportation service is not satisfactory. I am not finding fault with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; I am asking him to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to a condition that is absolutely unjustifiable, according to the evidence of men who are best competent to judge, namely, those who are in the business and are thoroughly conversant with every detail of it in the city of Montreal and elsewhere. There is a good deal of evidence here on this point that I might read, tout it is not my purpose to go into it just now. Furthermore, the Minister of Railways,	a few years
ago, increased the freight rates and charges	and changed	the quantity
making up a car lot. Formerly, from 20,000 to 25,000 pounds would make a car lot; that amount has been increased to about 30,000 pounds. In other words, a man who wishes to ship must have a greater bulk of fish before he can get the car rate; besides, the car rate is higher. I contend that in this respect the fishing interests of the Maritime provinces have been unfairly treated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall have much pleasure in calling the attention of the Minister of Railways to the criticism that my hon. friend makes, and of asking him to read in Hansard what the hon. gentleman has said. This whole matter, however, has been very fully discussed in the Committee of Marine and Fisheries, which will shortly be making a report to the House. No doubt there will be some discussion of the report, when this matter can be brought up and ventilated.

In reading from the Fisheries report, the minister, read an item which indicated that a refrigerator car service toy fast freight would be a sufficient substitute for the express service. I do not think the person who wrote that understood what he was talking about, be-



cause you cannot substitute the one lor the other. The express service .is for small packages, to he delivered at the 'different stations along the railway from the place where the fish is caught to the city of Montreal. The refrigerator car, however, that is made up at Halifax or Mulgrave, runs through without -stopping anywhere except to change engines at Campbellton and one or two other places. At these stops they do not allow any freight to be taken on or off, -so the refrigerator oar service can never take the place of the express service. We are without any express service on the Intercolonial railway that is any good. The express service that we have is in a car heated with steam pipes, and the fish which are put in a box of ice in that car arrive in Montreal in a bad condition, soft and unfit for the market. When the minister is discussing this matter with the Department of Railways, he .must insist on there being an express service as well as a freight service if he is desirous of giving the fish trade from the Maritime Provinces any chance.

If I have any objection to the view of the hon. member for Antigo-nish it is that he is entirely too mild in the opinions that he has expressed with regard to the liability of the Government for what evidently is their utter failure to encourage the fishing industry of the Maritime Provinces so far as a market is concerned. My hon. friend says that he does not blame the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; he blames the Minister of Railways. I think that the sooner we get rid of the idea that the head of one department may be very culpable and other members of the Government in no way to blame, the better. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is just as responsible and just as culpable as the M-inister of Railways in connection with this matter, and he must take the responsibility just the same as the Minister of Railways. The statement -made by the member for Antigonish and the member for Guysborough that there is really no express service for fish between the Maritime Provinces and Upper Canadian cities at the present time, is a surprising statement, and one that requires immediate attention. Some years ago, in order to encourage the securing of a market in the inland cities of Canada for the fish of the Maritime Provinces, an express service was established -so that the fish could be quickly delivered from the point of shipment to the upper Canadian markets. It was recognized that

it was desirable not only to have an express service on the Intercolonial railway, but that the Government should pay a portion of the charges made by the express companies. Now that has been done away with, and the Government is asking the fishermen to rely upon a fast freight service under which, as it was stated in the committee, fish cannot be delivered to the upper Canadian markets inside of eight days or so. That is calculated to interfere very much with the trade, and I do not think that the minister should put the matter off by telling us that in a few days there will be a report by the Fisheries Committee. The fact is not denied that the express service, which we have had in the past, has been discontinued. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) states it positively, and so does my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. W. Chisholm). We ought to have a better explanation from the minister than we have had yet as to why this backward step has been taken. My hon. friend the minister has been taking a great deal of credit to hirqself for the efforts that are being made to get a market for the fish of the Maritime Provinces. If report is correct, he has even taken steps to supply Canadian fish to the Canadian forces at the front, and yet here, with a market in the cities of -the upper provinces open to our fishermen, the Government has taken this backward step which those engaged in the fishing business say is exceedingly detrimental to their business.
Mr.- HAZEN: JMy hon. friend is mistaken entirely in this matter. We have practically the same express service in operation on the Intercolonial railway as that to which my hon, friend refers. We have the same service with regard to the carrying of fish from the Lower Provinces, and that it has not proved a failure is shown by the fact that the markets of Montreal, Toronto, and other Canadian cities, are to-day supplied entirely with Canadian fish, whereas previously they were supplied with fish from the United States. The arrangement under which that was brought about still continues, so far as freight and express services are concerned. What was referred to by my hon. friend fron Antigonish (Mr. William Chisholm) is a service that was instituted for the first time in 1913, and which was continued for a period of no less than two years, and not ' the service which my hon. friend from St.

John has in mind. In 1913, an arrangement was entered into by which an express refrigerator car was to leave Mulgrave on one day in each week, the Government guaranteeing that the contents of that car would be at least 10,000 pounds, and that they would pay any deficiency as between the weight of the contents of the car and a freight of 10,000 pounds. That car ran once a week from Mulgrave, and it was hoped and expected that the business would increase to such an extent that the amount of freight carried would exceed 10,000 pounds. The result was as stated by Mr. Found before the Maritime and Fisheries Committee. He says:
The service was started in 1913. It was under guarantee from the department that the earnings of the car would be at least those on
10.000	pounds. We got the express and the railway companies together to agree to reduce the minimum from 20,000 to 10,000 pounds. That, of course, did not relieve the department from paying one-third of the express charges on shipments in this car. During the year 1913, I am sorry I have not the record here, the results looked pretty good. There were only four or five days (I am speaking from memory and subject to correction) on which the minimum of 10,000 pounds was not being carried. But in 1914, for reasons which I will not attempt to go into at the present time, the shipments were not equal to that of 1913. A reference to page 15, in Roman numerals, of' the report of 1914-15, will show the details of that service. There were 34 trips made during that season, and of these 34 trips 18 had less than
10.000 pounds, running one as low as 2,700 pounds on the trip up to about 6,000, or a little more, not nearly up to, but very seriously under the 10,000 pounds which made the service an extremely expensive one. It will be easily seen that it was not doing what was expected of it. The railway company was very anxious to discontinue it,-	.
Which railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Intercolonial.
That means the Government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: It is on the statements of Mr. Brittain, the manager or secretary of the Maritime Fish Corporation, and a very able business man of large experience, that I place reliance, and he complains that this service was discontinued. The statement of my hon. friend the minister that the particular service discontinued was the one inaugurated by this Government ip 1913, does not militate at all against my statement that the Government has gone back upon a progressive policy which would have led to a greatly increased business. I understand that the service of which Mr. Brittain complains was discontinued only a few months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It did not operate in 1915 at all, except in the first month of the year.

It was continued for a couple of years at least, and it has been done away with. As I understand it, the objection is that while the fishermen, apparently, in many cases have preferred the fast freight service, that was because the Government was charging them so much for the fast express service. That was the reason; they could not afford to pay the charges for the fast express service. The result is that the Government is not encouraging the business as they started out to do, and, as everybody recognizes they ought to do, and the fast freight service is not giving satisfaction. I think it is unfortunate that the Government has taken this backward step, in order to save a little money. -
It is a backward step. They ought to have gone on encouraging the fast express service, given cheaper rates, made better arrangements with the express companies and

so encourage in the largest possible degree business, between the Maritime Provinces and the upper Canadian cities. I think the business is one of very grave importance and the Government might very well afford to lose some money upon the Intercolonial in order to encourage it.

I think the service
failed largely on account of the way in which it was dealt with. The minister himself has given the explanation why the service was not successful. The car only made thirty-four trips in the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A trip a week.
Mr. 'SINCLAIR: The daily train made 313 trips as it runs every week-day in the year. But, the business would never be a success unless a daily service is provided. The chances iare that the express refrigerator car would come a day after a storm, the fishermen could not go out to fish and there would not be enough fish to make up a shipment. If you are -going to make the business the success it ought to be, you ought to put an express car on every day, keep it on and give it ,a year's trial. This would give the dealers, especially the small dealers, a chance to do business which they have not now. The freight oar is the only available one for large shipments. 24,000 l'bs is the smallest shipment you can send by freight * car. There are very few dealers who can handle freight car shipments. This -shuts out the -small dealers altogether. That is a very large quantity and it excludes dealers who would take advantage of transportation facilities if they were available. I would like to see the minister try the experiment of putting a refrigerator car on the express train every day. Then the dealers would have an opportunity to work up a profitable business. It is getting near six o'clock, and if there is no objection, I would suggest that we get through with this item and perhaps another one.

I would like to ask the minister if he has received any petitions from the residents of Ingonish in the county of Victoria in regard to doing something to keep the harbour ice broken in the fall of the year. I was written to and told that they had sent a petition to the minister. It seems that in December, and early in January, the inner harbour freezes and if they do not get the ice broken they can not get out with their boats. It is quite open outside the bar but it freezes iniside. Last year they had the help of a steamer that went down there, not a Government steamer, and it was of great assistance to them because it broke up the ice and they were able to get outside. The patrol boats on the coast, if they have the necessary strength, could, with the greatest ease, keep this ice broken. I hope thS minister will take it into consideration. All that is necessary is for a boat to take a turn around the harbour every morning and break up the thin ice formed during the night so that the boats can get out. If that is not done the whole business of the place will be stopped.

It was not done by a Government steamer, but another steamer that happened to be down there on business. It was in the harbour and the master was good enough to run the boat around the harbour every morning and break up the ice for the people. It was worth thousands of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Bill No. 8, respecting the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company -Air. Morphy-in committee.
On section ,1-short title:

The first two Bills appearing on the Order Paper are of a contentious nature and likely to take up considerable time. Would it not be wise to deal with the other Bills before starting to discuss the first two?

We are here to transact business, and these Bills are the first on the Order Paper. I do not see any particular reason why they should not be dealt with now.
Air. ARA1STRONG: I wish to enter my most earnest protest against these Bills passing in their present form. They will interfere not only with provincial and national rights, but with a great proposition of the province of Ontario, one of the greatest propositions of its kind in the world. We have had, it is true, considerable discussion in the Railway Committee ih regard to the first two Bills on the Order Paper, the discussion some times continuing over several days. Before that committee there have appeared many representatives of the Ontario municipalities through which the hydro-radial lines are proposed to run, and every one of them has earnestly protested, against the passage of the Bills, advocating strongly that we

should defer their passage for at least one year, until the Ontario Government are alble to convince the members of this House not only that they are in earnest in regard to building the hydro-radials in the province of Ontario, but that those radials will be for the general advantage of the people of that province. Letters and telegrams of protest have been received^ and the reeves of the different municipalities between Toronto and Niagara Falls, the mayors of Toronto, Hamilton, Guelph, and of many other cities in the province have been doing their utmost to convince the members of the Railway Committee that it is in the interest of the people of the province of Ontario that we should not grant these charters. This is a letter from Niagara Falls, Ont., to the Chairman of the Railway Committee:
Dear Sir,-Enclosed you will please find copy of a resolution which was passed by the Niagara Falls Trades and Labour Council, which is self explanatory.
We would appreciate it very much if you will give the subject matter contained in the enclosed resolution your careful consideration.

Whereas the Mackenzie-Mann interests have had charters for railways granted to them by the Government, and
Whereas these charters have been in existence for a number of years, and the Mackenzie-Mann interests apparently have made very little effort to construct the railways said charters were granted for, and
Whereas the Hydro-Electric Railway Association of Ontario is an organization of the public, organized for the purpose of operating electric railways in the province of Ontario for the benefit of the public, therefore be it,
Resolved, that in the opinion of the Niagara Falls Trades and Labour Council there should be no renewal or extension of these charters granted in the province of Ontario for electric railways, and that no obstacle should be placed in the way of the Hydro-Electric to prevent it from being a success.
I might continue to refer to many municipalities which have sent forward most earnest protests. These are the names of the representatives of some of the municipalities who are anxious to do their utmost to defeat this measure: W. H. Myers, Secretary Stratford Public Utilities Commission; W. J. McCully, President Board of Trade, Stratford; E. C. West, town clerk, Campbell-ford; H. Mahonney, mayor, Guelph; B. Mc-Nichol, Water and Light Commissioners, Woodstock; A. G. Willson, Municipal Corporation Township of Bertie, Ridgeway, Ont.; H. iL. Barr, Secretary Board of Control, Hamilton; David Wagner, Secretary Trades and Labour Council, Niagara; Wm.
Stevens, Secretary Trades and Labour Council, Peterboro; Jos. Battle, Mayor town of Thorold; Water and Light Commission, town of Goderich; F. Stewart, Reeve Grantham Township Council, St. Catharines; C. H. Claus, Reeve Louth Township Council; W. B. Burgoyne, President Niagara District Hydro-Radial Union, representing all municipalities in counties of Lincoln, Welland and Haldimand; Thos. Hall, Trades and Labour Council, Guelph; John Morrison, city clerk, Woodstock, Ont. These are a few of the men who have sent most earnest protests against the passing of this charter. The Provincial Government of Ontario have also taken an interest in this question. They are responsible for placing before the people the great hydro-radial proposition; and after the success obtained in the Hydro-Electric organization, under which over $30,000,000 of the people's money in Ontario has been devoted to the development of hydro-electric power, and which is extending its operations in the eastern part of the province, it can be readily understood that they are most anxious that what is practically the key to hydro-radial development in Ontario should not be taken away. On the 8th March, the following resolution was passed unanimously by the Ontario Legislature. It was moved by Hon. Mr. Lucas, the Provincial Treasurer, and seconded by Hon. Mr. McDermott, the Minister of Public Works:
That this House reaffirms its opposition to the renewal of charters hy the Parliament of Canada to local electric railways in the province, and the removal of such railways beyond the jurisdiction of this Legislature, hy declaring that it will be for the general advantage of Canada.
This resolution, as I have said, was passed unanimously, which means that both the great political parties of Ontario stand behind this great Hydro-Radial proposition. That being so, it seems to me most, unfair for this Parliament to force upon them legislation which will materially interfere with the development of this great hydroradial policy. There is no question in my mind that it will be necessary for the local Government of Ontario to build the hydroradial lines between Toronto and Niagara Falls. And if you grant the Canadian Northern railway a charter,' to that extent you will interfere with the successful development ,of this scheme.	,
How so?
In this way. The estimated cost* of one of these lines is
What is the use of my bon. friend making this argument when the Government that he is supporting is going to pass this Bill P
This is not a Government measure. Members on this side of the House, as well as on the other side, are free to deal with these questions as they think best.
I approve of what the hon. gentleman is saying, but it is going to have no effect.

I hope that the statistics which I am placing on Hansard will have some definite effect, and that the hon. gentleman, with many other members on that side of the House, will support the hydro-radial proposition instead of the Canadian Northern Railway Company in this regard. I have called attention to the enormous amount of land grants and subsidies that have been granted to this railway company. We are told that they are not in a position to go ahead and build the road from Toronto to Niagara Falls. I do not feel like taking up the time of the committee to-night in going into the financial condition of the Canadian Northern railway ; I know that the members on both sides of the House realize that, so far as that is concerned the directors of that railway are not justified in building the road between Toronto and Niagara Falls, thereby expending $13,000,000. If the Canadian Northern Railway Company have $13,000,000 to expend on that road, how much better and wiser it would be for them to place proper rolling stook on their road to take care of their traffic, to build branch lines, for dozens of which they have received charters, and to take care of the traffic in the West. We have a Bill presented by the Minister of Railways for the purpose of compelling other railroads in Canada to place on the Canadian Northern Railway lines in the western provinces a sufficient amount of rolling stock to take care of the grain which the Canadian Northern railway is unable to move from the districts through which it passes. How unfair and unreasonable it is to ask the men who have settled along these branch lines, not only of the Canadian Northern railway but of other railway companies, which are just as guilty in that regard, to go to the expense of carrying their products to the main lines of railway in order to develop our great western plains. How much better it would be for those
settlers if the Canadian Northern railway were to spend the money in the betterment of their roads, in improving the terminals, in double-tracking where necessary, in placing proper rolling stock where it should be placed, in perfecting their system, and in entering into traffic arrangements with the Hydro-Electric on their line of railway from Toronto to Niagara Falls.
I cannot help but feel that the pioneer period of railway building in this country has passed, and that the development of our railways should be carried on under saner and wiser management. Let us put a stop to the latitude which we have shown in granting railway charters; let us not act so heedlessly and recklessly as we have done in the past in giving charters to individuals without investigation. Tens of millions of the people's money have been wasted through allowing railroads to parallel each other. Let us consider for a few moments the enormous amount of capital that has been wasted through railroads paralleling each other. Go to the province of Manitoba; it is estimated by railway statisticians that within a radius of ten miles of each railway, the duplication in the province amounts to 40 per cent. Take the situation in the East, if you will. Take the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Quebec to Moncton on which portion we spent over $35,000,000, thereby practically paralleling the Intercolonial railway.

It is a long distance
from the Intercolonial.
It may be, but the hon. gentleman is well aware that the ties on that portion of the Transcontinental are rotting and the rails are rusting.
I am not aware of anything of the kind; on the contrary the road is in splendid condition. The rails are first-lass, the ties .are good, and the roadway is in first-class condition.

That is very satisfactory from the hon. gentleman's standpoint, but we must remember that ties do rot and rails do rust. That road has been completed for some five years, and mighty little traffic has gone over it. How could it be otherwise than rusting and rotting? , .
That road has been completed for four or five years, and this Government has been in power for four or five years. Why have they allowed it to get into that condition?
Because of the reckless and wilful mismanagement of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the construction of the Quebec bridge.
This Government has been operating the road for several years.

That is true, but it is like many other burdens that were placed upon this Government. It was compelled . to operate this road and operate it at a serious loss to the people of Canada owing to the wilful and reckless mismanagement of hon. gentlemen opposite. We have gone on building railways far in advance of the needs of the districts through which they run and we should put a stop to it. In view of the fact that in Canada to-day we have invested in railways over $2,000,000,000," and taking into consideration the amount of traffic over tlhese roads, we must realize that, if we are to pay interest on the cost of building and of upkeep, freight and passenger rates in this country will not decrease for some time to come.
I was calling attention to the parallelling of railways. Go if you will to Edmonton, and you will see the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway parallelled between Edmonton and the mountains. Those of you who have travelled over them must realize that an enormous amount of money has been wilfully wasted in the building of these parallel roads. In England we find a very different state of affairs. We find that there they have a certain definite policy in regard to railway building and development, and that it is impossible for individuals, or for any body of men, to go ' before the Government and obtain a charter to build a railway without the charter coming before a competent board of men who are thoroughly conversant with railway statistics and with the needs of the district through which the railway is likely to pass. What they have accomplished in England during the last couple of years has been largely due to the fact that the railways are built through districts where they give the greatest service. The Railway Commission ought to have something to say, or, at least, they should be able to place before the Railway Commission definite statements of fact in regard to the needs of the' district through which it is proposed to build a railway. One of the questions that Parliament will have to deal with in the next few years will be the public ownership, control and

management of two great transcontinental railways in this country. It is well for us to look ahead in granting charters such as these now before the committee and see to it that we do not place any extra burdens on the people in that regard. We will not need to debate the question:	Shall we
build battle cruisers or submarines after this war is over, but we shall have to consider the question: Shall we build more railways without proper investigation by some tribunal which is not only independent but qualified to make such an inquiry?
Let me direct the attention of the committee for a moment to the Ontario Hydroelectric proposition. The Hydro-Electric Commission is not here asking for bonuses or subsidies. It is here asking for the simple right to build a railway, and it is opposing this charter, because it is likely to parallel the railway that it is compelled to build in order to develop its hydro-raidiai railway sclieme. The Ontario Government and the people of that province have decided in favour of hydro-electric development. In most of'the municipalities in Ontario to-day we find the hydro-electric service being developed and light, heat and power being furnished to the people at cost. There are very few municipalities to-day that will not hold up both hands in favour of hydro-electric development being carried on in conjunction with hydroradial development. Most of the municipalities which have been provided with light, heat and power by the Hydro-Electric Commission are anxious that these radial railways should be built. The HydroRadial Commission are now spending $4,251,000 on new terminals in Toronto. This has been voted by the people of Toronto and they are anxious that every assistance should be given them in the way of developing hydro-radials going into that city. The sum of $14,000,000 has been voted by municipalities to build hydroradial railways between Toronto and London and $5,000,000 of that $14,000,000 is to be devoted to the development of hydro-radials between Hamilton and Toronto. The sum of $4,700,000 has been voted for lines east of Toronto and there will be required $2,250,000 more to complete the acquisition of a satisfactory entrance into Toronto. Within the last two months the provincial government of Ontario have purchased 20 plants in the eastern portion of Ontario at a -cost of $8,000,000. They purchase these plants not only for the purpose of developing hydro-electric but for the purpose of developing

hydro-radials connecting with these different municipalities. We should do everything we can to assist them in this proposition. The proposition that is made through the charters you are asked to pass upon to-night will entail an expenditure of at least $13,000,000 for terminal rights of way, rolling stock and equipment from Toronto to Niagara Falls. The Provincial Government have a definite policy in this regard. The Canadian Northern Railway, on the other hand, has roving charters in Ontario to the extent of 680 miles. These Bills, if passed, will simply grant to the Canadian Northern Railway Company the right to hold up radio railway development in many parts of the province. While the Canadian Northern have these roving charters covering 680 miles of railway, it is true that we do not expect that any of these lines are going to be built in the near future. In fact, the Canadian Northern themselves admit freely, I understand, that they have no intention of building any of these railways. Then why should we renew these charters granting to them the right to cover 680 miles of territory on which the HydroElectric are now making surveys, and thereby interfere with the development of the Hydro-Electric scheme?
Is the" proposed Hydro-Electric to parallel the existing line that is owned by a Hamilton company, and which runs from Hamilton to Grimsby?

I remember the hon. gentleman asking the same question of Sir Adam Beck when the Bill was before the Railway Committee. Sir Adam Beck explained to him that the electric railway running out of Hamilton is only a rural railway running along the highway, while the hydro-electric railway will be built on their own property, purchased by themselves, and built on the highest standard as far as rails and ties are concerned, in order that they will be able to carry rolling stock quickly over that road. It will be impossible for them to take over the little line which the hon. member for Simcoe has referred to.
Then this proposition is to ruin an existing railway by competition?

That is what I might expect the hon. gentleman to say. Sir Adam Beck called the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that that was a local line, simply running on the highway, and that it would be impossible to expect that
any railway which would go through that district would not be likely to parallel it. It is only a short railway anyway.
Then, if it is no fault on the part of the Hydro-Electric to parallel an existing railway, what fault will there be if the Canadian Northern runs along there too?	'

It just makes one more. It makes it that much less possible for the Canadian Northern to expect that we will be able to carry on railway development in that district with a great deal of profit. I want to hurry along, because I have an important matter that I would like, to deal with. If my hon. friend from Simcoe will be good enough to leave me alone, I will get through all the quicker. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway have running rights over these railways. It is not going to interfere with Canadian Pacific development in that district.. That is an important matter to take into consideration. Another matter I want to call the attention of the committee to is that in the province of Ontario, and especially in the part from which I come, we have a number of the main lines of the great railways. While it is true that they are giving a very good service to the people who are living conveniently to those lines, it is also true that they build very few branch lines, and that it is practically impossible for the people in outlying districts to compel them to build branch lines or to serve local needs. There are many districts in western Ontario that are badly in need of just such lines as the hydro radial will give. A map of the surveys that has already been made shows that the hydro radial will run through districts that are now ten, fifteen and even twenty miles away from a railway, and which, if the intensive farming that is carried on there is to meet with any success, must have improved railway facilities. I have been endeavouring to show the needs of the hydro radial.
Is a bonus included among the needs of the hydro-radial? Are they asking for assistance from either the Federal or the Provincial Governments ?
That is one of the stock arguments of my hon, friend. The question was asked of Sir Adam Beck, and he was able to say that they had no intention of asking the Dominion Government for aid.
Oh, no, he did not. At a public meeting he said that he had had a promise of $3,500 a mile.
That was some time ago. I understand that they intend to proceed with, the development of the hydro radial whether they receive Federal assistance or not.
They can not do it.
I can not agree with my hon. friend. They are going to proceed without assistance from the Government, and undoubtedly they yrill make a success of the undertaking.
Let me just read from a report of the meeting of the hydroradial at God,erich.

I am sure the committee will be glad to hear from my hon. friend a little later on.' The Hydro is also of great help to the munition 9 p.m. factories in western and eastern Ontario. Furthermore, it will carry freight at cost.
The hour for Private Bills having expired, the committee rose and reported progress.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Department of the Interior-Scientific Institutions-Astronomical surveys, $260,000.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext:
['The matter will be given every consideration.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
Monday, April 3, 1916.']

We discussed this item at considerable length the other evening, and the minister said he would give us particulars as to how it is proposed to expend this amount, particularly with regard to the Geodetic Survey.

I have had a memorandum prepared by my deputy, who, unfortunately, has been taken ill, and been advised to take a holiday. It reads as follows:
The object of this survey is to provide accurately determined fixed points of reference, upon which surveys of all kinds may he based. It often happens that several surveys are made covering- the same ground, such as geo'ogical surveys, road or railway surveys, drainage surveys, military surveys, etc. Each of these surveys requires its datum as to level, and Its connection with known points, so that it may be'placed in its proper position on the general map. The first survey made expends labour and money to obtain these datums. There being no assurance that the proper standard of accuracy was reached in this survey, the sec-

ond survey makes a connection for itself, duplicating the work of the former survey. This is repeated, more or less, for each succeeding survey, and results in the aggregate to a very appreciable waste.
The Geodetic Survey aims to place permanent marks at convenient distances throughout the country, and to determine positions and elevations of these in the most accurate manner possible. This is the whole aim of the Geodetic Survey. It does not aim at the determination of the flow of Niagara or other rivers, though doubtless those surveyors engaged in such important work would find Geodetic Survey reference marks or bench marks, when available, most useful.
The operations of the Geodetic Survey are carried on by triangulation, and by precise levelling. The former determines the positions of points in plan, that is, in northing or southing, easting or westing. The latter gives the elevations The triangulation points have been found useful in the surveys of the Militia Department, and in the Hydrographic Surveys of the Naval Service Department. Inquiries have lately been made about them by the Engineering Department of the city of Toronto. They will be useful in any surveys that may be made in connection with city planning. The results of the precise levelling are of use to those making topographical surveys, such as the surveys branch of the Militia Department. They are much sought for by railway engineers and city engineers.
At many places not reached by triangulation of the Geodetic Survey, reference points are established by astronomical observation. Formerly this Was possible only where a telegraph line was available, and a large number of astronomical stations have been established by telegraph throughout Canada. They have been serviceable generally for the correction of maps, while in British Columbia they have been used largely for the laying out of the local system of survey. An application of wireless telegraphy has extended the scope of these observations, and it is now possible to determine longitudes, as well as latitudes, accurately in the most inaccessible regions. In the last two years the Observatory has established a number (13) of astronomical stations in the Ottawa river basin, in Ontario and Quebec, for the use of the Ottawa river survey, Department of Public Works. The advantage of sueh points is that they may be used to coordinate detailed surveys that are widely separated, and thereby to save the expense of the survey of intervening ground. The saving in this easily runs into the tens of thousands of dollars, while the expense of the observations is trifling.
. Mr. PUGSLEY:	What is the estimated
expenditure on the Geodetic Survey for the-coming year?
The survey of the Northwest began away back in the sixties, and milos and miles were .surveyed. Was not that before there was any item in the Estimates for a Geodetic Survey?
res.

Will the Geodetic Survey affect that territory?
Mr. ROCHE; No, we are not going to use the Geodetic Survey on that territory. I would refer my hon. friend to a debate that took place in the House a few years ago when he was a member of the then Government, when this question of the Geodetic Survey was brought prominently to the attention of the House by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who pressed very strongly upon the then Minister of the Interior the necessity of expending far more money in connection with this survey. I have his speech here, and I could, if I desired to take up the time of the House, show hon. members the necessity he gave for that expenditure.
Mr. PUGSLEY-:	There was no war on
then.

The minister agreed to a
certain extent with the reasons given, and the expenditure was somewhat increased during his term of office. There was quite a discussion on this question, all of the members urging the then minister to spend far more than he had been spending in the past on this -survey.
Does this survey affect the latitudes and longitudes of all the provinces as laid down by the established system of survey?

I do not think it does. It is, as the hon. gentleman knows, a species of survey that is the basis for the topographical survey and other surveys. Although the hon. member stated the other night that he had never found it of the slightest service in connection with the Public Works Department, nevertheless there are on file about fourteen applications from the Public Works Department to this branch for information in connection with the operation . of that department, and there are similar applications from the Department of Railways.

There are always some
scientific gentlemen who are searching for the undiscoverable, and I suppose they would be interested in that wonderful system of geodetic survey; they would naturally want to inform themselves. But, for all practical purposes, so far as immediate necessity is concerned, this item might very well stand over. The war is on, and every dollar that can be saved to the public treasury will be needed for the purposes oi
the country in connection with the war, for the payment of interest and pensions, and for the discharge of the numerous other obligations which are arising from day to day. This matter was pretty thoroughly discussed some little time ago when the minister had his Estimates before us, and he stated that of this $260,000, $125,000 would be used for the Geodetic Survey. I would move:

As I was Minister of the Interior for a period, and as the work of this Geodetic Survey was in progress during part of that time, it is perhaps necessary that I -should give a reason for voting for the amendment of tlhe hon. member for St. John. We are, Erom time to time, calling upon the Government to reduce expenditures rather than to increase taxation; and, taking that attitude, from time to time as the Estimates are under consideration we are bound to give instances in wlhieh we think the Government should reduce the expenditure., As having had responsibility and experience in regard to this matter, I have no hesitation in saying that, in my judgment, however desirable this expenditure may be under other circumstances, it is under existing circumstances an expenditure that can be cut out without injuring the well-being of the country now or in the immediate future.
In the address -made by the junior member for Halifax, he instanced the case of other countries where Geodetic Surveys had been made, but there was no comparison between those countries and Canada. He instanced Belgium. Belgium is a country as large as perhaps one or two Canadian counties, and the completion of a Geodetic Survey in a country such as Belgium, or even such as France or England, is a trfling matter as compared with -the undertaking to establish a Geodetic Survey throughout the v-ast area of this Dominion. A Geodetic Survey is simply a survey made for the purpose of establishing topography with

scientific accuracy and it has no necessary relation to immediate requirements as is the case in an ordinary survey. There may be circumstances under which it is right and pro/per to make an expenditure tor the purpose of establishing points and altitudes with scientific accuracy; but I am prepared to take full responsibility for saying that at this time, when we have such enormously increasing financial obligations to meet, the iGovemment which has charge of the affairs of the country is in the nature of things called upon to reduce expenditures wherever that reduction can be made without injury to the public service. In my humble judgment this is one of the instances in which such a reduction can be made without substantial injury to the public service.

I do not profess to be an astronomer or to be versed in scientific work, of any kind, but I have understood that there are advantages in carrying on

astronomical research in having observatories at high altitudes and in regions where the weather is in large proportion dry and the sky clear. If astronomical research were the purpose, I could appreciate a possible removal of the observatory from Ottawa to some point in the Rocky Mountains or the interior mountains of British Columbia. But we are informed that this observatory is located on Vancouver island within a few miles of the city of Victoria. Whatever advantage there may be on Vancouver island in the vicinity of the city of Victoria -and I am the first to admit that in many respects these advantages are not only great but many-they are neither in the line of clear sky and atmosphere nor in the advantage of high elevation. There are localities in British 'Columbia where these two requirements are to be met, but not where this observatory is located. The reason given by the minister that it was on account of the more desirable condition of atmosphere seems hardly to hold, because even though the condition of atmosphere near the city of Victoria may be measurably good, it cannot be as good as at other points in the interior of British Columbia, where immensely higher elevation and a much clearer atmosphere could be secured. I am sure the committee would be glad to hear a further explanation of the reasons why the observatory has been located on Vancouver island.

Investigations had been carried on by the staff for many months prior to the location of the observatory at its present site. Dr. Plaskett visited all the different points where experiments were being conducted. Medicine Hat was one of the points; others were at Ottawa, on the prairies, and at the site which has been selected. The report states that better work and more work all the year round can be done at the present site than at any other point in Canada.
The minister has the report there?

I had it with me when the Estimate was placed before Parliament for the first time. I think I read from it; I do not know whether I placed the whole report on Hansard or not. Other points, of course, besides clearness of atmosphere were considered; in any -case, the experiments carried on by day and by night convinced those in charge that they could do more and better work at the site selected. An influential delegation waited on me

urging the purchase by Canada of a new telescope, which, it Was claimed, would be a splendid advertisement for the country, and would in its operation attract scientists from all parts of the world. There have been many inquiries in this connection; the telescope has caused amongst scientific men a great deal of favourable comment. I understand that it will be the best and most creditable telescope that there is in existence. Probably since the contract for it was let a telescope has been built in another country which is about as large, if not a little larger, than ours, but, up to the time the contract was let, this telescope was by far the largest in existence. After investigations extending over many months, Dr. Plaskett and Dr. King had no hesitation in recommending that the telescope be located at Saanich.
Had the conditions been ias favourable in the city of Ottawa, they would have much preferred to locate it here, as there would be advantages, this being the capital of the Dominion. But the matter was given very careful consideration and there was no lack of investigation before deciding to place it where it is.

I would not like to make any remarks that would be considered unnecessarily controversial, but I may say that, on the face of the record, it appears to me that the establishment of the observatory where it is, and under the circumstances, was rather with the view of making provision for a continuation of employment for scien-

tific gentlemen at an increased cost to the country, and with some regard to political advantage in a certain locality rather than with the view of pursuing scientific research.

selves boards of trade. I would ask the hon. gentleman if that committee was not the suggestion of the Saanich board of trade?

After a very great deal of research by certain gentlemen this observatory has been located at Saanich. It strikes me that the conditions of a very desirable place to live synchronized marvellously with the suitable location for an observatory.

It is not impossible, but it. is somewhat striking. It must be admitted that such institutions, when established purely for scientific research, are generally placed at high altitudes and in localities where there is an abnormally clear atmosphere, both of which conditions are found in certain parts of British Columbia, but are not found at Saanich. I am not desirous of repealing the item or of breaking down the arrangement made. Of course, the arrangements having been made, it. would be folly not to carry them out. I am making what I claim to be a fair criticism as to the policy and what we assert to be the extravagance which the Government have shown in this particular case. My hon. friend has said that had the suggestion come to him to interview the Government on this subject after the outbreak of the war he would have thought it inopportune. But in the year 1913, although the war had not broken out, the condition of financial buoyancy which had prevailed up to the fall of 1912 had ceased, and we were in a condition that certainly was anything but financially prosperous, and that fact might very well have appealed to he Government, because it was evident that

we had entered upon a period when economy rather than expenditure would be desirable. The point I dpsire to make is that this expenditure was undertaken at a time when' the financial condition should have directed the Government to lesser and not greater expenditure. As to the necessity of keeping up our end, so to speak, with other countries, I can hardly agree with my hon. friend that, because Chili, Bolivia, or some other country, sees fit, because pf its abnormally favourable conditions, atmospheric and otherwise, for astronomical research, to undertake large expenditures in this connection, when it has not so many calls upon it as Canada has, this country should be compelled to keep pace with it. When my hon. friend says that we should keep pace in research work with every other country on earth, even though we are in a period of depression, I maintain that the point is not well taken, and that the Government which he so ably supports is fairly to be judged guilty of extravagance in this matter.

I would move that this amount be reduced by $250,000.

I have listened to the
Minister of the Interior explaining the reasons for the different items mentioned by the hon. member for St. John and setting forth why they were of the amounts appearing in the list that was read. It is a remarkable fact that under the Administration of my hon. friend, while settlement on the land has decreased by one-half, the expenditure to secure that settlement has a little more than doubled since my hon. friend's Government took office. The only reason that can be given for that state of affairs is that the Government has administered the department extravagantly and without regard to the results achieved. In 1911 there were 44,000 homestead entries, and the Estimate for immigration was, I think, $915,000. While settlement on the land has decreased year by year, until this year there will not be more than 20,000 homestead entries, the expenditure for the purposes of immigration increased from less than $1,000,000 to over $2,000,000. Last year it was a little less than $2,000,000, and this year it is somewhat more than a million and a half. That is to say, with only half the number of homesteads taken in this 'year, when there is no possibility of securing immigrants from Europe, and when there is every reason for every measure of economy that can be instituted, the minister's Estimates of this year is 50 per cent larger than it was in the year 1911. With settlement 50 per cent less, his expenditure is 50 per cent more. There is no way to meet 
such a condition, except by motion to strike out. [DOT]
We do not wish to hamper immigration effort, but we certainly expect that immigration effort shall be well directed, and that reasonable economy shall be used. The expenditure, on the one hand, and the results on the other, show that there has not been economy or efficiency. It is true that the returns show that a large number of immigrants came into the country during a number of years, but the minister will not say, nor will any member of the Government say, that the money spent on immigration was spent for the purpose of bringing into this country persons other than those who would, directly or indirectly, settle upon the land. He will certainly not say that the money was spent for the purpose of bringing in labourers or artisans to compete with the labourers and artisans who are taxpayers of Canada. He will say, as he has already said, that the purpose of the expenditure on immigration is to bring in people who will either settle on land of their own, or work on land held by other people. Judged by that standard, his immigration effort must be considered a failure.
In regard to farm help, we have it on the authority of the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that it was absolutely impossible to get farm help in the province of Ontario. The immigrants brought out were not farm help, and the results of homesteading in the West show that they were not homesteaders. Therefore, instead of claiming credit for bringing out such a large number of immigrants, my hon. friend will have to explain to the country why those immigrants came when they were not required in the process of developing the country. In regard to the matter of extravagant expenditure, a return was tabled last session, in response to an inquiry as to the number of employees of several departments who had been appointed or dismissed, and the return showed that in the Department of the Interior 309 dismissals had taken place, that 374 officials of the department had resigned, and that 1,651 had been appointed, making a net increase of 968 officials in the Interior Department since my hon. friend's friends took office.
I have given figures which prove that the results achieved under the smaller expenditure were more in the interest of the country and bended more greatly to its development, than the results achieved under my hon. friend's larger expenditure. I have shown that, while this occurred, he has enormously increased the number of

officials in the service of the department. Therefore, I claim that the charge of extravagance and inefficiency against the administration of this department is maintained, and that the motion of my hon. friend from. St. John to strike out some part of this expenditure is well warranted.
Motion of Mir. Pugsley negatived: yeas, 9; nays, 22.
Administration of Chinese immigration-salaries, $28,000.

Will the minister explain where these Chinese are situated?

The merchants do not pay the head tax?
No.
[DOT] What proportion of the head tax is paid into the Dominion treasury, and what proportion to the provinces?

Fifty per cent of the net proceeds?	*

If I am in order in discussing another matter under this item, I would like to ask the minister for some information regarding a regulation that was>
passed in August or September last year, instructing the agents of the department to *interfere with Newfoundlanders entering the province of Nova Scotia. . We have a great many people from Newfoundland coming into Cape Breton to work in the mines. They come in the summer, work seven or eight months, then go home and come back to Nova Scotia again. Our mine managers find them a very excellent class of people to employ in the mines. Last year we were very much startled to find that there was a regulation put into force to prevent them coming into Canada, and it caused a great deal of ill-feeling in the island of Newfoundland. I think the regulation was withdrawn, but I would like to know from the minister why this new departure was entered upon. It is not desirable that we should create any disturbance between ourselves and the people of Newfoundland. Of course, away out in Manitoba and British Columbia they do not feel it very much, but we regard, Newfoundlanders very much as part and parcel of ourselves, because the distance between us is very small, and a great many Newfoundland people live in the town in which I reside. We find them excellent citizens and good people to associate with. It created a good deal of disturbance and inquiry, particularly when the war was on, many Newfoundlanders going to the front, not only from Canada, but from Newfoundland itself. If there is any satisfactory explanation that the minister can give I think it would be desirable that it be given here, so that these people and the Government of Newfoundland would know why Newfoundlanders were discriminated against in this way. Did any complaint come from our part of the country and what is the reason for passing this regulation?	.

The hon. gentleman speaks as if he were under the impression that a

special regulation tad been passed to prevent Newfoundlanders coming into Canada. People coming into Canada during the winter months are supposed to have $50 in cash in their own rights, and during the summer months $25. This regulation was put in force for a short time against Newfoundlanders, during my absence from Ottawa, on representations from certain people to the department that there were sufficient labourers in Nova Scotia unemployed to meet all the demands, and that mining men were bringing over Newfoundlanders to work in the mines. It was by reason of these representations that the department enforced the money qualification, not only against Newfoundlanders, but aganist people coming .from the British Isles, or any other country. We sent an officer down to inquire into the situation, owing to protests being received against the enforcement of the money qualification in respect to Newfoundlanders, an investigation was held by this officer and he advised that we should admit Newfoundlanders without insisting on the money qualification. It was only for a short time that this regulation was in force and we now treat Newfoundlanders as ordinary returning Canadians.

I have received from Mr. Ben C. Saloway, who lives in my riding, a letter in regard to immigration matters. I do not propose to read it but there are one or two suggestions to which I would like to call the attention of the minister. Mr. Saloway is an Englishman who, during the last Government's term of office, was in England as immigration agent and he is a very observant man. He writes ime that he thinks that large numbers of the industrial class of Englishmen will come over to Canada and settle. He points out that, 'homesteads being much fewer in number than they were, these men of the industrial class are perhaps scarcely fitted to go out in the newer countries situated long distances from railways. He makes the suggestion that, there being large areas in. the hands of speculators near railways, the department might make some arrangement with the holders of these lands to sell them on more reasonable terms than those at which they now offer them for sale. He points out that if these men attempt to purchase lands on the terms now offered it will only mean ruin to them. The views of Mr. Saloway on this matter are set forth in the Montreal Star of the
